units.Jeremiah 43:1: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, the Lord’s word came to me:

units.Jeremiah 43:3: Perhaps Judah’s house will hear all the calamities I intend to bring upon them, so that they turn from their evil way and I may be merciful toward their injustices and sins.

units.Esther 3:13a: This is the copy of the letter: “The great King Artaxerxes writes the following to the rulers of the hundred and twenty-seven territories from India to Ethiopia and to the district governors subject to them:
units.Esther 3:13b: Having ruled many nations and gained control of the whole inhabited world, I have wished—not exalting myself through the boldness of authority, but always conducting myself with greater fairness and gentleness—to establish the lives of my subjects in perpetual calm, to provide a civilized kingdom open to travel to its furthest limits, and to renew the peace desired by all people.
units.Esther 3:13c: When I asked my counselors how this might be brought to completion, Haman, who excels among us in sound judgment, has demonstrated unchanging goodwill and firm loyalty, and has received the second honor in the kingdom,
units.Esther 3:13d: pointed out to us that among all the tribes throughout the inhabited world a certain hostile people is intermingled, opposed in its laws to every nation, continually disregarding the kings’ decrees so as not to accept the shared administration that we direct blamelessly.
units.Esther 3:13e: We have therefore understood that this nation alone stands in continual opposition to every person, differing through its strange observance of laws, showing ill will toward our affairs, and accomplishing the worst evils so that the kingdom may not enjoy stability.
units.Esther 3:13f: We have therefore commanded that all those indicated to you in the writings of Haman, who is appointed over our affairs and is our second father, be destroyed root and branch, with wives and children, by the swords of their enemies, without any pity or sparing, on the fourteenth of the twelfth month, Adar, of the present year,
units.Esther 3:13g: so that those hostile both formerly and now may go down violently to Hades in a single day and thereafter leave our affairs stable and undisturbed for all time.”
units.Esther 3:14: The copies of the letters were posted in every territory, and all the nations were ordered to be ready for that day.
units.Esther 3:15: The matter was also hurried forward in Susa. The king and Haman were drinking heavily, while the city was troubled.
units.1 Maccabees 5:45: Judas gathered all Israel in Gilead, from small to great, with their wives, their children, and their belongings—a very great company—to go into the land of Judah.
units.1 Maccabees 5:46: They came as far as Ephron. It was a large, exceedingly strong city on the road, and there was no way to turn aside from it to the right or left, but only to pass through its midst.
units.1 Maccabees 5:47: The people of the city shut them out and blocked the gates with stones.
units.1 Maccabees 5:48: Judas sent to them with peaceful words, saying, “We will pass through your land to go to our land. No one will harm you; we will only pass through on foot.” But they would not open to him.
units.1 Maccabees 5:49: Judas ordered a proclamation through the company that each should encamp in the place where he was.
units.1 Maccabees 5:50: The men of the force encamped. He attacked the city all that day and all that night, and the city was given into his hand.
units.1 Maccabees 5:51: He destroyed every male with the edge of the sword, uprooted the city, took its spoils, and passed through the city over the slain.
units.1 Maccabees 5:52: They crossed the Jordan into the great plain opposite Beth-shan.
units.1 Maccabees 5:54: They went up to Mount Zion with gladness and joy and presented whole burnt offerings, because none of them had fallen before they returned in peace.
units.Deuteronomy 25:19: And it shall be, when the Lord your God gives you rest from all your enemies round about you, in the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession to inherit, that you shall blot out the name of Amalek from under heaven. You shall not forget.
units.1 Maccabees 6:32: Judas withdrew from the citadel and encamped at Beth-zechariah opposite the king’s camp.
units.1 Maccabees 6:33: The king rose early in the morning and set his army moving rapidly along the road to Beth-zechariah. The forces prepared for battle and sounded the trumpets.
units.1 Maccabees 6:34: They showed the elephants the blood of grapes and mulberries to ready them for battle.
units.1 Maccabees 6:35: They divided the beasts among the phalanxes. Beside each elephant they stationed a thousand men armoured in chain mail, with bronze helmets on their heads, and five hundred picked cavalry were assigned to each beast.
units.1 Maccabees 6:36: They were in position beforehand wherever the beast was; wherever it went, they went together and did not leave it.
units.1 Maccabees 6:37: Strong, covered wooden towers were on them, secured by devices upon each beast. On each were four fighting men and its Indian driver.
units.1 Maccabees 6:38: He stationed the remaining cavalry on either side, on the two wings of the army, threatening the enemy and shielding the phalanxes.
units.1 Maccabees 6:40: One part of the king’s army spread out on the high mountains and others on the low ground. They advanced securely and in order.
units.1 Maccabees 6:41: Everyone who heard the sound of their multitude, the march of the multitude, and the clash of weapons was shaken, for the army was exceedingly large and strong.
units.Nahum 2:1: Look, upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace! Celebrate your feasts, Judah; repay your vows. For they will no longer pass through you into decay. It has been completed; it has been removed.
units.Nahum 2:2: One who breathes into your face has come up, rescuing from affliction. Watch the road; hold your waist firm; act courageously with great strength,
units.Nahum 2:3: because the Lord turned away Jacob’s arrogance, as Israel’s arrogance; for those shaking them out shook out both them and their vine branches; they ruined
units.Nahum 2:4: the weapons of their might from among people, mighty men playing in fire. The reins of their chariots are on the day of his preparation, and the horsemen will be thrown into uproar
units.Nahum 2:6: Their nobles will remember and flee by day; they will weaken on their journey, hurry to the walls and prepare their defenses.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: imperial conquest and pride
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Alexander's plundering of many nations and lifted-up heart are comparable to the Assyrian ruler's lofty pride and boast of seizing the inhabited world and plundering nations. The connection is the conjunction of expansive conquest, spoil and self-exaltation; Isaiah's ruler, explicitly identified as Assyrian, is not identified with Alexander.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: He passed through to the ends of the earth and took the spoils of a multitude of nations. The earth became quiet before him; he was exalted, and his heart was lifted up.

target_units.text: When the Lord has finished doing all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, He will bring judgment upon the great mind—the ruler of the Assyrians—and upon the height of the glory of his eyes.
For he said, “By strength I will act, and by the wisdom of understanding. I will remove nations’ boundaries, plunder their strength and shake inhabited cities.
I will seize the whole inhabited world in my hand like a nest, and lift it like abandoned eggs. There is no one who will escape me or contradict me.”

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Literary parallel: communal mourning across generations
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Maccabees depicts elders groaning and young women weakened in Israel's mourning; Lamentations depicts Zion's elders in dust and sackcloth and Jerusalem's leading virgins brought to the ground. Both give communal calamity a visible expression among elders and young women, without describing the same catastrophe.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: Rulers and elders groaned; young women and young men grew weak, and the beauty of women was changed.

target_units.text: Daughter Zion’s elders sat on the ground in silence. They put dust on their heads and girded themselves with sackcloth. They brought the leading virgins in Jerusalem down to the ground.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: altered beauty in calamity
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Maccabees includes the changed beauty of women in the account of national mourning. Isaiah portrays fragrance, head adornment and decorated clothing giving way to dust, baldness and sackcloth. The comparison concerns the loss of an adorned appearance in calamity; Maccabees does not specify Isaiah's individual changes.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: Rulers and elders groaned; young women and young men grew weak, and the beauty of women was changed.

target_units.text: Instead of sweet fragrance there will be dust; instead of a belt you will gird yourself with a cord; instead of golden head adornment you will have baldness because of your deeds; instead of the tunic with purple at its center you will gird yourself with sackcloth.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Literary parallel: bridal life interrupted by communal distress
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Maccabees brings the bridegroom and the bride in her bridal chamber into Israel's lament. Joel calls the bridegroom from his bedroom and the bride from her bridal chamber into the gathered community, where priests weep for the people. Both extend communal distress into bridal life, though Joel commands an assembly and Maccabees reports mourning.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: Every bridegroom took up a lament, and the bride sitting in her bridal chamber mourned.

target_units.text: Gather the people; consecrate the congregation. Choose elders; gather infants nursing at breasts. Let the bridegroom leave his bedroom and the bride her bridal chamber.

In the midst of the altar’s platform the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say, “Spare Thy people, Lord, and do not give Thine inheritance to reproach, for nations to rule over them, so that they do not say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: incense to foreign gods throughout urban life
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The incense at house doors and in squares follows the establishment of pagan altars in Maccabees. Jeremiah similarly depicts Judah's cities burning incense to foreign gods and Jerusalem's many exits associated with incense altars to Baal. Both present foreign worship spread through inhabited places; the doors and squares are not equated with Jeremiah's exits or assigned his named deity.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: At the doors of the houses and in the squares they burned incense.

target_units.text: And Judah’s cities and those dwelling in Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to whom they burn incense. Will those gods save them in the time of their evils?
For your gods were according to the number of your cities, Judah; and according to the number of Jerusalem’s exits you set up altars to burn incense to Baal.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Narrative parallel: sacred writings cut apart and burned
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The persecutors tear the books of the law and burn them; Jehoiakim cuts columns from the roll of Jeremiah's words and burns the whole roll. Both express hostility to divine instruction by physically dividing and burning its written document. The law books and Jeremiah's prophetic roll are different writings in different incidents.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: They tore apart the books of the law that they found and burned them with fire.

target_units.text: When Jehudi read three or four columns, the king cut them off with the scribe’s knife and threw them into the fire on the brazier, until the whole roll was consumed in the brazier’s fire.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Wisdom parallel: praised remembrance of righteous deeds
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The praise of Judas joins deeds that gladden Jacob to a memory that remains a blessing. Proverbs describes the memory of righteous people as accompanied by praises, in contrast to the extinguished name of the impious. The proverb illuminates the favorable remembrance expressed in the tribute to Judas.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: He embittered many kings and gladdened Jacob by his deeds; his memory is a blessing for ever.

target_units.text: The memory of righteous people is with praises, but the name of the impious is extinguished.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: accepting God's will amid readiness to face death
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Judas concludes his willingness to face death in battle by affirming that Heaven's will will be done. After Paul declares his readiness to die for the Lord Jesus, his companions yield with the words that the Lord's will be done. The shared movement is from readiness for mortal danger to acceptance of divine will; the speakers and conflicts differ.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: But whatever the will in heaven may be, that He will do.”

target_units.text: Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
Since he would not be persuaded, we became silent and said, “Let the Lord’s will be done.”

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: human plans subject to divine will
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Judas prepares for the coming battle but leaves its outcome to the will in heaven. James corrects confident plans for tomorrow by saying that both continued life and action depend on the Lord's will. Both qualify human intention by divine will, without equating Judas's battle preparation with the trading plans James addresses.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: But whatever the will in heaven may be, that He will do.”

target_units.text: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this city, spend a year there, trade, and make a profit”—
you who do not know what tomorrow brings. What is your life? For you are a vapor, appearing for a little while and then disappearing.
Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we shall both live and do this or that.”

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Narrative parallel: smoke reveals a military reversal
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The detachment looking from the mountain recognizes its side's defeat from the visible smoke of the burning camp. At Ai, inhabitants and Joshua's force see the city's rising smoke, and Israel turns against Ai's men. In both battles smoke makes the capture and burning of a position visible to forces outside it; the tactics and the subsequent ability to flee differ.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: They saw that their men had been routed and that the camp was being burned, for the visible smoke made plain what had happened.

target_units.text: Ai’s inhabitants looked behind them and saw smoke rising from the city toward heaven. They no longer had anywhere to flee, this way or that.
Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had taken the city and that its smoke rose toward heaven. They turned and struck Ai’s men.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: priestly integrity and devotion to the law
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Judas chooses blameless priests devoted to the law for the cleansing of the holy places. Malachi's account of faithful priestly service joins truthful law and freedom from injustice to the priest's duty to guard knowledge and provide law. This connects the qualities sought in the chosen priests with the described priestly vocation, not with a second account of their appointment.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: He chose blameless priests devoted to the law.

target_units.text: A law of truth was in his mouth, and injustice was not found on his lips. Directing his way in peace, he walked with Me and turned many back from injustice.
For a priest’s lips will guard knowledge, and people will seek law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the Lord Almighty.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: a coordinated plan to destroy Jews in one day
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: The report from Gilead describes an arranged assault intended to destroy the confined people in a single day. Esther's letters likewise schedule the destruction of the Jews on one day. The connection is the concentrated timetable for destroying a Jewish population, while the local siege plan and empire-wide decree remain distinct.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: They were also confined in the other cities of Gilead. The enemy had arranged to attack the strongholds the next day, seize them, and destroy all these people in one day.

target_units.text: Letters were sent by couriers into Artaxerxes’s kingdom to wipe out the race of the Jews in a single day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, and to plunder their possessions.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Narrative contrast: treatment of those lagging on a journey
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Judas gathers those who lag behind and encourages the company on the road to Judah. Deuteronomy recalls Amalek attacking the weary people at Israel's rear on the journey from Egypt. The concrete contrast is care for stragglers against exploitation of the rear's vulnerability; Judas is not presented as consciously reenacting that earlier journey.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: Judas gathered those who lagged behind and encouraged the people along the whole road until he came into the land of Judah.

target_units.text: Remember what Amalek did unto you in the way, when you came forth out of Egypt,
how he withstood you in the way, and smote your rear, those who were weary behind you, when you were hungry and weary; and he did not fear God.

final_retained_full_triples.relationship: Imagery parallel: an army flashing like fiery torches
final_retained_full_triples.rationale: Maccabees likens sunlight reflected from the army's golden and bronze shields to torches of fire shining on the mountains. Nahum likens the appearance of chariots in the roads and squares to fiery torches and flashing lightning. The shared comparison conveys the dazzling appearance of military equipment, while the equipment, setting and movement differ.
final_retained_full_triples.source_text: When the sun flashed upon the golden and bronze shields, the mountains flashed from them and shone like torches of fire.

target_units.text: in the roads, and the chariots will be thrown into confusion and entangled in the squares; their appearance is like torches of fire and lightning flashing past.

deferred_source_units.source_text: He summoned his distinguished officers, who had been brought up with him from his youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive.
deferred_source_units.reason: The newly read Daniel 11:3-4 does describe a powerful king and a divided kingdom, but it does not name Alexander or his officers and differs from the voluntary lifetime division described here. The general partition motif alone was not retained as a sufficiently particular connection; the earlier uncertain identification remains unresolved.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: He summoned his distinguished officers, who had been brought up with him from his youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive.
unresolved_candidates.reason: Both passages mention a king and division of his kingdom, but Daniel's unnamed kingdom is shattered and divided toward the four winds, whereas Alexander summons his officers and divides his kingdom while alive. The read text does not establish the proposed historical identity, and this broad partition resemblance was not retained as a separate thematic pair.

target_units.text: A powerful king will arise, exercise great lordship, and do whatever he wishes.

When he arises, his kingdom will be shattered and divided toward the four winds of heaven, not according to his might or the lordship with which he ruled. His kingdom will be removed, and he will teach others these things.
